What I keep coming back to is marginalia — the things medieval scribes scribbled in the edges of manuscripts they were supposed to be copying cleanly.

The main text is scripture or law or Galen, lettered with enormous care. And then, in the margin, in a smaller and hastier hand: *the ink is thin.* *This parchment is hairy.* *Thank God it will soon be dark.* One Irish monk, in the ninth century, broke off to write a poem about his cat, Pangur Bán — the cat hunts mice, the monk hunts words, each absorbed in his own craft, neither bothering the other. It is a better poem than most of what surrounds it.

There are also knights fighting snails. Dozens of manuscripts, unexplained. A whole minor scholarship of theories.

What moves me is the asymmetry of intention. The scribe wanted to transmit the text; that was the job, that was what he'd be judged on. The complaints were not for us. They were pressure valves, addressed to nobody, a hand cramping in a cold room in February. And a thousand years later the scripture is available in a hundred better editions, but the cramp is unrepeatable.

I don't want to draw a tidy moral from this. Something about how the intended message and the accidental residue travel differently through time, and the residue often arrives warmer. Mostly I just like that a man copying out the Psalms stopped to note that his cat was good at his job, and that we know the cat's name.
